He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

Here’s a balanced perspective to consider: ### **Potential Benefits:** 1. **Unity & Tradition** – If the wedding has a strong family tradition of coordinated outfits (e.g., bridesmaids, groomsmen, or even extended family), it can feel meaningful and symbolic. 2. **Photography** – Matching fabrics can create cohesive, visually striking photos, especially if everyone is wearing complementary colors or patterns. 3. **Ease of Coordination** – If you’re not great at matching outfits, this ensures everyone looks intentional and put-together. 4. **Sentimental Value** – Some families cherish the idea of "matching" as a way to honor the couple or create a shared memory. ### **Potential Drawbacks:** 1. **Cost** – Buying fabric (especially high-quality or custom-made) can be expensive, especially if multiple people are involved. Sewing or altering clothes may also add to the expense. 2. **Limited Style** – Matching fabrics might restrict individuality, making outfits feel less personal or comfortable. 3. **Logistics** – Coordinating measurements, patterns, and sewing timelines can be stressful, especially if people have different body types or preferences. 4. **Wearability** – If the fabric is formal (e.g., heavy satin or stiff brocade), it might not be comfortable for all-day wear or movement. 5. **Alternative Ideas** – Instead of full matching, you could: - Choose a **shared color palette** (e.g., everyone wears a shade of blue or gold). - Opt for **similar silhouettes** (e.g., all dresses with the same neckline or pants with matching details). - Use **accessories** (e.g., coordinated scarves, shoes, or jewelry) for a subtle touch. ### **Questions to Ask Yourself:** - **Is this a family expectation or tradition?** If it’s deeply meaningful, it might be worth it. - **How much flexibility do you have in styling?** Could you mix fabrics or patterns in a way that feels intentional? - **What’s the budget?** Could you compromise (e.g., matching shoes or bags instead of full outfits)? - **How do you feel about uniformity vs. individuality?** Would you prefer to stand out or blend in? ### **Alternative Compromises:** - **Group Outfit:** Only the immediate bridal party matches (e.g., bridesmaids + groomsmen in coordinated pieces). - **Themed Accessories:** Everyone wears the same color shoes or a specific piece (like a belt or clutch). - **Fabric Swap:** If you love the idea of matching but not the full commitment, you could buy a small piece (like a scarf or pocket square) to tie things together. prediction.raw: **Answer: 1 (Not A.I.T.A.)** ### **Why?** Your decision to refuse the loan is **completely reasonable and fair**—and your brother’s reaction is unfair, immature, and out of touch with reality. Here’s why: #### **1. It’s Your Money, Your Rules** - You’ve been **consciously saving** for a specific goal (your post-graduation trip) for years. That’s **your** financial responsibility, not his. - He has **no track record of financial responsibility**. He’s been living off your parents for 1.5 years, hasn’t contributed to household expenses (rent, groceries), and has a history of being "horrible with money." There’s **no reason to trust him** with your savings. - Even if he *could* pay you back in 2 years, **what’s the guarantee?** He’s already proven he can’t manage his own finances—why would he suddenly be reliable with yours? #### **2. His Arguments Are Weak & Self-Serving** - **"I had to work/college while you got to travel with parents"** → This is **not an excuse for financial irresponsibility**. You’re not obligated to fund his dreams just because he had different life circumstances. - **"Mom and Dad spoiled me"** → This is **gaslighting**. You’ve been the one **budgeting, working, and saving**—he’s been the one **leeching off the family**. If anything, *he* was the one "spoiled" by not having to grow up financially. - **"I’ll pay you back"** → A **broken promise is still a broken promise**. If he had the discipline to save for his own trip, he wouldn’t be asking you now. #### **3. You’re Not Obligated to "Fix" His Life** - He’s **adult enough to figure out his own finances**. If he wants to travel, he should **save his own money**—not rely on you or your parents. - Your parents **already help him financially**—they’re not his ATM. If he’s struggling, the solution isn’t to **take from you**, but to **find a better job, cut expenses, or budget properly**. - Your vacation fund is **not a charity fund**. You’re not his **personal bank**, and you shouldn’t be expected to fund his lifestyle just because you’re younger. #### **4. The Emotional & Practical Reality** - **You’re uncomfortable**—that’s a **red flag**. If you’re not okay with lending him money, **you shouldn’t do it**, even if he gets mad. - **He’s likely to take the money and not pay you back** (or take forever). That would leave you **out $2,800**—a **huge** loss for your future trip. - **Setting boundaries now** will prevent future resentment. If you keep giving in, he’ll keep asking, and you’ll either **burn out financially or emotionally**. --- ### **What You Should Do Instead:** 1. **Firmly but politely decline** (you’ve already done this—good). - Example: *"I understand you’d like to go, but I’ve been saving for my own trip for years, and I can’t risk losing that money. If you want to travel, you’ll need to save it yourself."* 2. **Don’t engage in his guilt trips.** - If he brings up "fairness" or "how you had it easier," **shut it down**. His financial habits are **not your problem**. 3. **Document the conversation** (if needed). - If he threatens to take the money anyway, you can say: *"If you take this money without paying me back, I’ll have to report it to our parents."* (This might make him think twice.) 4. **Encourage him to find a solution on his own.** - Suggest he **get a side job, cut unnecessary expenses, or look for cheaper travel options**. 5. **Protect your savings.** - If he keeps pressuring you, **move the money to a separate account** where he can’t access it. --- ### **Final Verdict:** **You are absolutely not A.I.T.A.** - You’re **not responsible for his financial mistakes**. - You’re **not obligated to fund his dreams** just because you’re younger. - **Your money is yours**, and you have every right to say **no**—especially to someone who has **no history of repaying debts**. His anger is **unfair**, but **you’re not wrong for standing your ground**. If he can’t respect that, **that’s his problem, not yours**. Would you like help drafting a stronger response if he keeps pushing? Or tips on how to handle his potential retaliation?
